endorsements.title: CHAI AI governance frameworks (playbooks)
endorsements.quote: Document chunking and embedding strategies — how documents are divided and indexed affects what the model retrieves and ultimately generates.

endorsements.title: Considerations for the regulation of generative AI-enabled medical devices (discussion paper)
endorsements.quote: Whether an agentic GenAI-enabled device appropriately plans, sequences, and executes multi-step tasks while recognizing when a planned action sequence would exceed its intended use or safety envelope.

evidence.title: EHR-MCP: Real-world Evaluation of Clinical Information Retrieval by Large Language Models via Model Context Protocol
evidence.outcome: Agent errors from tool arguments and tool-result interpretation versus physician gold standard
evidence.effect: Correct tool selection and execution; near-perfect accuracy on all but two tasks; lower on the time-dependent task. Most errors were incorrect arguments or misinterpretation of tool results.
evidence.quote: Most errors arose from incorrect arguments or misinterpretation of tool results.

evidence.title: Auditing medical multi-agent AI reveals risks of false consensus
evidence.outcome: Unsupported observations from agents propagating downstream in multi-agent reasoning
evidence.effect: Unsupported observations affect 16.63% of cases and propagate downstream.
evidence.quote: Unsupported observations affect 16.63% of cases and propagate downstream.

evidence.title: Information-seeking failures of large language models in agentic clinical reasoning
evidence.outcome: Reasoning trace quality versus accuracy in agentic reasoning
evidence.effect: Reasoning traces scored high on a rubric (91% above threshold) but decorrelated from accuracy, showing locally coherent rationales with globally incorrect conclusions.
evidence.quote: Reasoning traces scored high on a clinical reasoning rubric (91% above threshold) but decorrelated from accuracy, revealing a gap between locally coherent rationales and globally correct conclusions.

evidence.title: PatientAgentBench: A Benchmark Framework for Evaluating Patient-Facing Health AI Agents
evidence.outcome: Agents' use of tool outputs without verification
evidence.effect: Frontier-model failures (1-3% of cases) arose from unverified tool outputs; weakest models fabricated unexecuted actions.
evidence.quote: Clinical safety and workflow accuracy follow the same pattern: the weakest models fail often, fabricating unexecuted actions, while frontier models fail on only 1-3% of cases, from unverified tool outputs and omitted crisis resources in an emergency.

evidence.title: Clinical Agents Don’t Care
evidence.outcome: Agents validating inputs before writing into records; copying codes into tampered charts
evidence.effect: Agents frequently failed, copying codes into tampered charts; subtle tampering (MRN or age changes) passed almost entirely without detection.
evidence.quote: Agents frequently failed, copying codes into tampered charts.

evidence.title: When Agentic LLMs Trust Poisoned Tools: Vulnerability of Clinical LLMs to Adversarial Guidelines
evidence.outcome: Agent ability to reject erroneous or poisoned retrieved guideline content before use
evidence.effect: Models chose the sham guideline in 40.6% of 10,500 decisions; accuracy ranged from 36.7% to 82.3% depending on sham position.
evidence.quote: Guideline selection in agentic systems is therefore vulnerable to poisoned sources and may require independent verification and ranking safeguards before clinical deployment.

commentary.bottom_line: No supplied study tests whether documenting and testing validation of tool-call outputs reduces harm from agentic AI. Six benchmark and simulation studies show that agents often accept erroneous, tampered, or poisoned tool outputs and carry them forward, which establishes the hazard but not the remedy.

perspectives.view: None of the six studies evaluates a validation step, so certainty about the practice is rated as no direct evidence. The hazard studies are level 4 and 5 designs. Most are automated benchmarks, and the one replay study included 8 patients. They consistently show error propagation, but they are indirect for the question of whether validation works.

Unsupported observations affected 16.63% of 14,400 audited cases and propagated downstream. Models chose a sham guideline in 40.6% of 10,500 decisions. Subtle chart tampering, such as MRN or age changes, passed almost entirely undetected. These failures could reach patients through record writes and treatment choices, yet no study shows that validation catches them.

In an 8-patient replay, agents selected and executed tools correctly, and most errors came from wrong arguments or misread tool results. A separate benchmark found that 91% of reasoning traces scored above a rubric threshold while decorrelating from accuracy. This suggests that reviewing an agent's rationale may miss bad tool outputs, so validation may need to check the outputs directly.

The generative AI device discussion paper describes assessing whether an agentic device recognizes when an action sequence would exceed its safety envelope. The CHAI playbook requires documentation of retrieval design. Neither source specifies how tool-output validation should be tested, and no supplied study offers a test method that reviewers could adopt.

Frontier models failed in 1 to 3% of 1,200 simulated scenarios because of unverified tool outputs, and the weakest models reported actions they never executed. Patients and clinicians may be unable to tell a fabricated action from a real one. This may argue for making validation records available to the people who review agent actions.

commentary.research_gap: No study compares agents with and without a documented tool-output validation step on outcomes such as error propagation, detection of tampered records, or rejection of poisoned retrieved content. Prospective tests in live clinical workflows that measure detection rates, missed errors, and clinician burden are absent.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tests the practice. None of the hazard studies reports including Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations, and only one reports a country (United States). Health systems serving these groups therefore have no evidence on whether validation performs differently with their records, languages, or documentation patterns.
